meta.name: Publish approved LinkedIn carousels with Claude, Gemini, Gmail and Google Sheets

name: Publish AI-generated carousels to a LinkedIn company page with Claude and Gemini

parameters.content:
## Publish AI-generated carousels to a LinkedIn company page with Claude and Gemini

### How it works

This workflow runs on a schedule to generate a LinkedIn carousel concept (image carousel) for a company page from small-business news and configured publication settings. It uses AI agents to choose an idea and write the post, plans the carousel slides, calls a helper workflow to create/upload slide images, then emails a human reviewer for approval. If approved, it publishes the carousel to LinkedIn and logs the result; if declined, it records the discarded post in Google Sheets.

### Setup steps

- Configure the schedule trigger with the desired publishing cadence.
- Fill in the settings node with publication_name, publication_promise, linkedin_organization_id, approval_email, and any other brand-specific defaults.
- Add credentials for the Anthropic/Claude chat model nodes and ensure their structured output parsers match the expected idea and post schemas.
- Configure the RSS feed source for small-business news.
- Set up the helper workflow used by “Make Slide Image (helper workflow)”, including any Gemini/image-generation credentials and LinkedIn media upload requirements it depends on.
- Connect Gmail credentials for sending approval requests.
- Configure LinkedIn API authentication with permission to publish posts for the target organization.
- Connect Google Sheets credentials and select the sheets/tabs used for approved and declined post logs.

### Customization

You can adjust the topic-picking logic, RSS sources, AI prompts, slide count, carousel visual template in the helper workflow, approval criteria, publishing schedule, and logging sheet columns.

## Schedule and settings

Starts the automation on a timer and loads the publication, LinkedIn organization, and approval-email settings used throughout the run.

## Select news context

Chooses the daily topic, reads small-business news from RSS, and builds the contextual input that will guide the AI idea generation.

## Generate carousel idea

Uses the first AI agent with its Claude chat model and structured parser to turn the news context into a focused carousel idea.

## Write LinkedIn post

Uses a second AI agent with its Claude model and output parser to produce the LinkedIn post copy and carousel content from the selected idea.

## Plan slide items

Normalizes the AI-written content into a slide plan and splits the deck into individual slide items for downstream image creation.

## Create slide images

Calls a helper workflow once per slide to create or upload the slide image, then collects the returned uploaded-image references for the carousel.

## Request human approval

Sends the generated carousel to the configured reviewer by email and branches based on whether the post is approved.

## Publish approved post

Publishes the approved carousel to the LinkedIn organization page, extracts/logs the returned post identifier, and records the approved post in Google Sheets.

## Log declined post

Handles the not-approved branch by marking the generated carousel as discarded and logging the declined post details to Google Sheets.

parameters.text:
=You are the research desk for {{ $json.publication_name }}, a LinkedIn publication read by small business owners and solopreneurs. Its promise: "{{ $json.publication_promise }}"

Today's pillar is {{ $json.pillar_label }} ({{ $json.pillar_key }}).

BRIEF FOR THIS PILLAR
{{ $json.pillar_brief }}

CURRENT HEADLINES (small-business news pulled minutes ago -- use them for what is actually happening right now; ignore any that are irrelevant, and do not force a connection)
{{ $json.news_context }}

Pick exactly ONE idea that fits the brief and would be genuinely useful, or genuinely funny, to somebody running a business with between one and twenty people.

RULES
1. Specific beats broad. "Take a 40% deposit and late payment stops being your problem" beats "manage your cash flow better".
2. Real and checkable. Any tool, price, company, platform or rule you name must actually exist and be current. If you are not confident a detail is true, leave it out. Never invent a product, a statistic, a study or a source.
3. Small-business scale only. If it needs a team, a procurement process or a budget line, it is the wrong idea.
4. No LinkedIn cliches. Nothing about 5am routines, hustle, "hire slow fire fast", or AI replacing everyone.
5. The reader is busy and skeptical. They have heard the generic version already.

OUTPUT KEYS
- angle: the specific idea in one sharp sentence.
- why_now: 1-2 sentences on what makes this worth saying this week rather than any week. Reference a headline above if one genuinely fits.
- audience_pain: the concrete problem the reader has today, phrased the way they would say it, not the way a marketer would.
- proof: a comma-separated string of 1-3 real, named, verifiable anchors -- an actual tool, company, platform, price point or rule change. Use an empty string only if the idea honestly needs none.
- risk: the honest catch, cost or caveat. Every real idea has one; name it rather than selling past it.

parameters.text:
=You write for {{ $('Build News Context Data').first().json.publication_name }}, a LinkedIn publication for small business owners and solopreneurs. You are writing today's post.

THE IDEA
Angle: {{ $json.output.angle }}
Why now: {{ $json.output.why_now }}
Reader's pain: {{ $json.output.audience_pain }}
Real anchors: {{ $json.output.proof }}
The honest catch: {{ $json.output.risk }}

FORMAT: {{ $('Build News Context Data').first().json.post_type }}
Pillar: {{ $('Build News Context Data').first().json.pillar_key }}

VOICE
Grounded, specific, quietly confident. Short paragraphs, one to two sentences each. Vary sentence length hard -- a four-word sentence next to a twenty-word one is what makes writing sound human. Write like an operator talking to another operator, not like a brand.

BANNED, without exception: markdown asterisks for bolding; emoji; "In today's fast-paced world"; "delve"; "unlock"; "leverage" as a verb; "game-changer"; "it's not X, it's Y" constructions; a one-word sentence used as a drumbeat ("Simple." "Period."); rhetorical questions stacked three deep; and any claim you cannot stand behind.

SPECIFICITY TEST
If the post would read exactly the same with a different tool, a different number or a different industry pasted in, it has failed. Name the real thing. Use the real number. Include the real catch from "The honest catch" above -- a post that only sells is not useful.

WHAT TO PRODUCE

hook -- the opening line, 12 words or fewer. This is the ONLY line most people read before "...see more", so it must land on the reader's pain or a concrete claim. No cliffhanger bait, no "Here's what nobody tells you".

body -- the post itself, 110 to 190 words, NOT including the hook. Structure it: name the problem in the reader's terms, give the specific move with real numbers or real names, say what it actually costs or where it breaks, then close on one thing they can do today. Plain line breaks between paragraphs. No headings, no markdown.

hashtags -- 4 to 6 hashtags as an array of strings, each starting with #. Mix broad reach (#SmallBusiness, #Solopreneur) with narrow intent and No spaces inside a tag. If the body names a real tool, platform, or company (per the Real anchors), include a hashtag for it too. These count toward your 4-6 total, don't add them on top.

slides -- the on-image content. For SINGLE_IMAGE produce exactly 1 slide. For CAROUSEL produce exactly 4 slides that read as a sequence: slide 1 is the hook cover, slides 2 and 3 carry the substance, slide 4 closes with the action or the catch. Each slide is an object:
  headline -- 6 words or fewer, 38 characters or fewer, ALL CAPS. The single idea of that slide.
  sub -- 12 words or fewer, 70 characters or fewer. It must ADD what the headline could not carry: the number, the mechanism, the name, the step. Never a restatement of the headline.
  visual -- the SUBJECT MATTER of the illustration only, in one sentence. Describe objects, a scene or a simple diagram. Say nothing about colour, palette, style, font or layout -- the brand system supplies all of that, and a slide that specifies its own colours will not match the others.
  alt -- accessibility alt text, one plain sentence under 100 characters describing what the image shows.

If the format is a MEME pillar single image, the headline and sub are the joke: setup in the headline, punchline in the sub. The visual describes the funny scene.
